Listening intently for the vibrations of larger animals, the little amphibians group together for safety in the thick mud of the river 
bank. Only after hours of nothing but the buzz of insects will they venture out into the water and try their best to harpoon unwary 
frogs and fi sh, practicing for the lethal aim they'll need to survive into adulthood.
Curious and excited about every new experience that the Fenlands have to offer, a pebbleback calf is a stark contrast from the more 
dour and stoic adults. With their pebble-like osteoderms not fully developed, the young mammal cannot yet withstand the bite of 
many predators and, so, relies on its agility to escape and rush back to the safety of its herd.
Hundreds of little fennfi stle tadpoles hatch from their cluster of eggs and swim towards the safety under the shade at the river's 
edge instinctively. Hiding beneath lily pads and slow moving ruske, they dart out to attack minnow and other minuscule fi sh. When 
confronted with larger creatures, they are quick to scurry and batter away the more persistent ones with their tails.
Wading in the water as close as possible to their herd, the fi rst few seasons of a gurubara's life is when it is at its most fraught with 
danger. Since the calming algae has yet to bloom within its short fur, the pups look to be the most delectable of prey, and any careless 
wandering young gurubara can quickly fi nd themselves snatched up by the many predators that haunt these lethal waters.
